name: Atlassian
summary: Atlassian, which makes Jira, Confluence and Trello, publishes how it interviews engineers: a coding interview, a system design interview, a manager interview and a separate values interview, usually with someone from outside the team. Candidates commonly report that the values interview carries real weight, and Atlassian says a hiring committee reviews the interviewers' feedback before a decision.
rounds: Technical interviews: coding and system design
looks_for: Clear reasoning about trade-offs in code and design
How you collaborate and communicate, including with people outside engineering

questions.text: Tell me about a time you shared bad news openly.
covers: What the news was and who needed to hear it
Why you shared it early and plainly instead of softening or delaying it
How people reacted and what was done about the problem

questions.text: Tell me about a time you balanced speed with doing it right.
covers: The deadline pressure and what doing it right meant in that case
What you shipped first and what you deliberately held back or fixed later
How it worked out, and whether you'd strike the same balance again

questions.text: Tell me about something you changed for the better at work.
covers: What wasn't working and who it affected
How you got others on board rather than changing it alone
What improved, with a number or a clear before-and-after

questions.text: Tell me about a time a customer problem made you change your team's plans.
covers: The customer, the problem and how you heard about it
What you dropped or delayed, and how you agreed that with your team
What the customer got and what you learned about planning

questions.text: Tell me about a team success you're proud of. How did you help others do their best work?
covers: The goal and who was on the team
Credit to others, plus a clear account of your own part
How you supported teammates: reviews, unblocking, sharing knowledge

questions.text: Tell me about working with teammates in other time zones. How did you keep work visible and decisions clear?
covers: The setup: who was where and what you were building
Written habits you used: docs, tickets, decision notes, async updates
A moment it nearly went wrong and how you fixed it

questions.text: How would you design notifications for an issue tracker like Jira, so people hear about changes that matter without being flooded?
covers: Clarifying who gets notified and through which channels
Events flowing through a queue, with user preferences and batching or digests
Handling bursts such as bulk edits, and measuring whether people find it useful

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd design a shared page editor where several people can edit the same page at once.
covers: How edits are sent and merged, and what happens when two people change the same text
Saving versions so changes can be undone or reviewed
Keeping it fast for large pages and working when a connection drops

questions.text: Walk me through how you'd structure the code for a simple rate limiter so it's easy to change and test.
covers: A clear interface first, then one algorithm such as a token bucket
Separating the limiting logic from storage and time, so it can be tested
Edge cases: bursts, many users, and running on more than one server

questions.text: Walk me through a past project: who you worked with, the hardest technical problem and the business reason for the work.
covers: Why the business needed it, in a sentence
The hardest technical problem and the options you weighed
Who you worked with and how you'd do it differently now

questions.text: A release you shipped has broken a feature for a large customer. What do you do in the first hour, and afterwards?
covers: Limiting the damage first: roll back or switch off the change
Telling the customer and your team honestly what is happening
A blameless review afterwards and the fix that stops it recurring

questions.text: Why Atlassian? Which of its products have you used, and what would you improve in one?
covers: A reason linked to the team or product, not only the brand
A real experience with Jira, Confluence, Trello or another product
One specific improvement and who it would help

questions.text: Which Atlassian value means most to you, and when have you acted on it?
covers: One value, named once
A short, true example from your own work
Why that way of working matters to you

tips: The values interview carries real weight: prepare a story for each value.
Atlassian's engineering guide says interviewers care more about how you reason through trade-offs than about a missing line of code, so talk through your choices.
The coding interview covers code design as well as data structures: think about naming, structure and how you'd test what you write.
In system design, ask about users, reliability and cost before drawing boxes, and expect follow-ups that change the constraints.
Values interviewers often come from outside engineering, so keep stories free of jargon. Credit your team, then be clear about your own part.
In the manager interview, say so if you don't know something; Atlassian's own guide recommends it.
